newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Ukraine FM calm over Belarus/Russia union proposal.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine FM calm over Belarus/Russia union proposal.

text.p: Ukrainian Foreign Minister Hennady Udovenko said on Tuesday he recognised Russia and Belarus's right to unite but warned Moscow to respect Ukraine's own choice to join whichever alliance it wished.

Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Monday sent a letter to his Belarussian counterpart, Alexander Lukashenko, saying that both states should consider the idea of a referendum over unification "in one form or another."
"Every country...has the right to form an alliance with other countries," Udovenko told reporters during a two-day visit to Hungary.
"However, we would like other states to acknowledge the fact that we have the right not to join and it is important that other states should not have the right of veto."
Udovenko was speaking after talks with his Hungarian counterpart Laszlo Kovacs which focussed on the two countries future relationship with both the European Union and NATO.

Russian officials have made it plain that the Kremlin sees the threat of a union with Belarus as a useful tool in its losing battle against NATO plans to grant membership to countries from the former Soviet bloc.
Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic are the leading contenders for early membership of the alliance.
Ukraine has not asked for membership but does participate in the alliance's Partnership for Peace friendship programme and hopes to win security guarantees from NATO.
"Ukraine respects Hungary"s right to join NATO, but insists its own national security needs are taken into account during NATO expansion," Udovenko said.
Sergei Shakhrai, deputy head of the Kremlin administration, said on Monday unification between Russia and Belarus could be the best response to any NATO expansion move.
On Tuesday Kovacs struck a conciliatory note on Yeltsin's overtures to Lukashenko, which have received a warm response from Minsk, the Belarus capital.
"There are some statements (out of Moscow) which have a threatening tone to them and cannot be considered as adequate answers to NATO expansion," he said.

"But this is an internal affair of the two countries and has no connection with NATO expansion -- if the leadership and the population of these two countries make such a decision in a democratic way this entirely their affair," Kovacs said.

Yeltsin's move steals the thunder from nationalist and communist opposition politicians at home when Yeltsin is under pressure over his health problems and a budget crisis which has left millions of people without pay for several months.

The same politicians are also pushing for a more hardline attitude to Ukraine over the status of the Crimea -- which used to be part of Russia but which Stalin handed to Ukraine in 1954 -- and its main Black Sea port of Sevastopol.

Tensions between Russia and Ukraine over the issue came to the surface last month when Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma denounced the Russian parliament for laying claim to Sevastopol as a Russian city.
"Not everyone in Russia has learned to accept Ukraine as a sovereign state yet," Kuchma said.
The Russian government has denied it has any designs over Sevastopol and the Ukrainian governent is looking to Yeltsin to reinforce this position.
Udovenko described current relations with Russia over Crimea as "difficult" but the Russian president's recovery from his current bout of pneumonia could ease tension.
"We hope President Yeltsin returns to his office as soon as possible and that this will enhance a better solution of these questions," he said.
